title: Nerf!
summary: Josh and Chuck (with the iHeart intro voice co-hosting) explore the history of Nerf, the toy brand. They cover the uncertain origin of the word "nerf" (racing nerf bars on off-road vehicles, and a gaming usage from Ultima Online), the 1969 Nerf ball invented by Rin Geier (Reynolds) and cut with heated wire, the Nerf football developed with Fred Cox and John Maddox via injection molding, the 1980s ownership changes (Kenner, Tonka, Hasbro), the Lonnie Johnson Super Soaker link and the Nerf blaster era, concerns about 1980s toy-gun police shootings, the modding and cosplay communities, Human v. Zombies games, Nerf Action Experience Centers, and the hosts' spring tour dates. Includes an intro banter, several ad breaks, and a closing tour promotion in place of listener mail.

segments.title: Opening banter and Venice Beach skate park
segments.summary: The hosts open with shout-outs to listeners and friends, then Josh describes watching skateboarders at Venice Beach being mocked for 'nerf tricks', which leads into the episode topic.

segments.title: Origin of the word nerf
segments.summary: The hosts dispel false origin claims (French for nerve, and an acronym for non-expanding recreational foam). Josh explains that nerf bars on racing and off-road vehicles were the basis of the name.

segments.title: Nerf bars, foam padding and Nerf foam products
segments.summary: The hosts describe foam padding on roll bars as the root of the idea, with a marketer applying the term to foam balls. Nerf products are generally polyurethane foam, and the hosts discuss the low-tech appeal of the brand and its cultural popularity.

segments.title: Nerf in gaming slang
segments.summary: The hosts describe the gaming usage of nerf, from Ultima Online developers weakening overpowered swords, and make a joke about nerfing Bo Jackson.

segments.title: Invention of the Nerf ball in 1969
segments.summary: Rin Geier, who had invented Twister, developed a foam ball using packing foam cut with heated wire, and it was licensed after Milton Bradley and Parker Brothers passed. Early ads promoted it as an indoor ball, and it sold heavily in its first year.

segments.title: Nerf football, Fred Cox and injection molding
segments.summary: John Maddox proposed a field goal kicking game, and Vikings kicker Fred Cox suggested a light foam football. Parker Brothers licensed the idea, and injection molding made the Nerf football and basketball in 1972. The hosts mention other products such as tabletop pool and the boomerang.

segments.title: Ad break
segments.summary: A short sponsor break between segments.

segments.title: Corporate ownership of Nerf
segments.summary: The hosts trace Nerf's ownership through Parker Brothers, Milton Bradley, Kenner, General Mills and Tonka, and Hasbro's purchase of Tonka in 1991.

segments.title: Lonnie Johnson and the Super Soaker
segments.summary: Inventor Lonnie Johnson, while working on a cooling device, accidentally produced a pressurized water blast and saw a squirt gun opportunity. Larami licensed it as the Power Drencher, renamed Super Soaker in 1991. Nerf's first blaster was the Blast-A-Ball in 1989.

segments.title: Nerf blasters and the 1990s shift
segments.summary: After Hasbro acquired Super Soaker's owner, Nerf adopted pressure-based blasters, starting with the Sharpshooter. The hosts link the shift to 1990s extreme culture and to the 1980s police shootings of kids with toy guns, which led Nerf to design non-gun-looking blasters.

segments.title: Nerf modding, cosplay and military styling
segments.summary: Nerf guns took on military styling, and in 2003 Nerf introduced tactical rails that let users mod blasters. The hosts discuss the modding community and the Titan and Rival Nemesis, plus Adam Savage's modding video.

segments.title: Nerf modding community and makers
segments.summary: The hosts describe modders as tinkerers and engineers rather than dangerous subculture, mention Luke Goodman and Spitfire Products making 3D-printed Nerf sniper rifles, and note how enthusiasm concentrated among fans.

segments.title: Ad break
segments.summary: A sponsor break between segments.

segments.title: Hasbro disclosure and Nerf games
segments.summary: The hosts note Hasbro owns Trivial Pursuit, which makes it part of their own family, then introduce Nerf battles that can run for hours or days.

segments.title: Human v. Zombies and Nerf melee weapons
segments.summary: The hosts describe Human v. Zombies games on college campuses, with bandana-marked humans, zombies tagged by Nerf darts, and fifteen-minute sit-outs. They also mention Nerf melee weapons and collector value.

segments.title: Nerf prices and similar toys
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Nerf price points and off-brand ammo, then compare with Gotcha, laser tag, and the paintball fad of the 1980s.

segments.title: Nerf slogans and ammunition changes
segments.summary: Josh notes Nerf's slogan 'It's a Nerf or nothing' and the shift toward firmer rubber-like ammunition with greater range. Earlier darts had been low-velocity.

segments.title: Nerf responsiveness and Action Experience Centers
segments.summary: The hosts praise Nerf for responding to modders and Human v. Zombies players with tactical rails and zombie-themed lines, then discuss Nerf partnerships and the Nerf Action Experience Centers in Hong Kong, London and New Jersey.

segments.title: Wrap-up
segments.summary: The hosts decide to end the topic and skip listener mail.

segments.title: Tour dates and sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts promote spring tour dates in Washington DC, Medford (Boston area), and Toronto, and invite listener email at stuff podcast at iHeartRadio dot com.
